name: Mehrgarh culture
info: Mehrgarh, near the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, Pakistan, is one of the earliest known farming and herding sites in South Asia, lived in from a Neolithic village (c. 7000 or c. 5250 BCE) until about 2600–2000 BCE.

facts.homeland: The Kacchi Plain of Balochistan, Pakistan, near the Bolan Pass, west of the Indus River, between Quetta, Kalat and Sibi; six mounds on a site of about 2 km²; the Sibri cemetery about 8 km away
facts.period: Period I (aceramic Neolithic) 5250–4650 BCE by recent radiocarbon dating, formerly pre-7000–5500 BCE; Period II 4650–4000 BCE; Period III (Chalcolithic, Togau phase) 4000–3500 BCE; Periods IV–VI 3500–3000 BCE; Period VII 2600–2000 BCE; Period VIII at Sibri
facts.known: early farming of barley and wheat; herding of sheep, goats and cattle; mud-brick houses and granaries; drilled teeth (proto-dentistry); female clay figurines; wheel-made Togau pottery with geometric designs; button seals; the oldest known lost-wax casting
facts.sources: Excavations by the French Archaeological Mission in the Indus Basin (1974–1986 and 1997–2000), about 32,000 artefacts; radiocarbon dates, including on teeth; dental studies of the burials; genetic studies of lactose tolerance in India

t: Mehrgarh is one of the earliest known places in South Asia where people farmed barley and wheat and herded sheep, goats and cattle, living in mud-brick houses.
Over thousands of years its villagers moved from a Neolithic life without pottery to wheel-made decorated wares, copper working, faience beads and seals.
Whether its farming came from the Near East or grew locally is debated, and so is the age of its first village: c. 7000 BCE in the older dating, c. 5250 BCE in the newer.
dyk: Eleven molar crowns from nine adults buried at Mehrgarh had been drilled during life: the oldest evidence of its kind, taken as a sign of a long tradition of proto-dentistry among early farmers.
ev: A small farming village is founded in the north-east corner of the site, by the older and the newer dating of Period I
In Period II pottery appears, with glazed faience beads, more detailed figurines and the first button seals
In Period III Togau pottery with geometric designs, made on a potter’s wheel, appears, and settlements multiply across the region
The site is largely abandoned in favour of the fortified town of Nausharo, during the Indus Valley Civilisation
The French Archaeological Mission in the Indus Basin, led by Jean-François and Catherine Jarrige, discovers the site
Excavations recover about 32,000 artefacts from six mounds
A study in the journal Nature reports drilled human teeth from the Neolithic graveyard

sections.origins:
Mehrgarh is a Neolithic and Chalcolithic archaeological site on the Kacchi Plain of Balochistan in Pakistan, near the Bolan Pass and west of the Indus River, between the modern cities of Quetta, Kalat and Sibi. “Mehrgarh culture” is a name for the way of life found there, taken from the site itself. The site was discovered in 1974 by the French Archaeological Mission in the Indus Basin, led by Jean-François Jarrige and Catherine Jarrige. It was excavated continuously from 1974 to 1986 and again from 1997 to 2000; material has come from six mounds, and about 32,000 artefacts have been collected.

Archaeologists divide the occupation into eight periods. The earliest settlement, a small farming village in the north-east corner of the site, was dated by Jarrige to before 7000 BCE, with Period I placed at pre-7000–5500 BCE. Recent radiocarbon dating on teeth by Mutin and Zazzo puts Period I between 5250 and 4650 BCE instead, so the founding of the village is now given as either c. 7000 or c. 5250 BCE. The aceramic Neolithic of the region was first called the Kili Gul Muhammad phase, and Periods I–III are considered contemporary with the site of Kili Gul Mohammad.

How farming began here is debated. Mehrgarh was influenced by the Neolithic of the Near East, with similarities in domesticated wheat, early farming, pottery, other artefacts, plants and herd animals. Jarrige, however, argues for an independent origin: given its originality, he concludes that Mehrgarh had “an earlier local background” and was not a “backwater” of the Near Eastern Neolithic. Lukacs and Hemphill suggest local development, with continuity of culture but a change of population between the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods.
sections.society:
The first farmers at Mehrgarh were semi-nomadic people who grew wheat and barley and kept sheep, goats and cattle. They built houses of unbaked mud brick, most with four internal subdivisions, stored their grain in granaries and lined large baskets with bitumen. Their crops included six-row barley, einkorn and emmer wheat, jujubes and dates. Mehrgarh is probably the earliest known centre of agriculture in South Asia, and the earliest evidence of cattle herding in South Asia, dated to 7,000 years before the present, comes from the site.

Over time crafts took a growing share of effort. Residents of the later periods (5500–2600 BCE) worked at flint knapping, tanning, bead production and metalworking, and Period II, the ceramic Neolithic, shows much manufacturing activity and more advanced techniques. In the later periods an area set aside for the pottery industry was laid out on mound MR1. In Period III the remains spread over around 100 hectares, but Jarrige concluded that this was not one large settlement: several villages or settlement clusters had shifted and partly overlapped across several centuries.

Graves give a glimpse of social life. In Period I more goods were left with men than with women; as time passed the goods became fewer, were limited to ornaments, and more were left with women. The teeth of the dead tell of care for the living: eleven molar crowns from nine adults had been drilled during life, which the authors of a 2006 study in Nature took as evidence of a long tradition of proto-dentistry in early farming cultures of the region.
sections.beliefs:
What its people believed can only be inferred from graves and figurines. Many Period I burials held elaborate goods: baskets, stone and bone tools, beads, bangles, pendants and occasionally animal sacrifices. One ground stone axe was found in a burial; it and others from the surface are the earliest ground stone axes from a stratified context in South Asia. In Period II two flexed burials were found with a covering of red ochre over the body.

Two kinds of burial are known. Some individuals were enclosed singly within narrow mud walls; collective burials had thin mud-brick walls, and inside one the skeletons of six different people were found. The bodies in the collective burials were laid in a flexed position, east to west. Between 4000 and 3300 BCE children’s bones were placed in large jars, as urn burials.

Clay figurines are the other main clue. The oldest ceramic figurines in South Asia come from Mehrgarh; they occur in all phases of the settlement, even before pottery. The earliest are simple, but by 4000 BCE they show their characteristic hairstyles and prominent breasts. Until Period VII all were female; male figurines appear only then and slowly become more common. Many of the women hold babies, and they have been interpreted as depictions of a mother goddess. Because that identification is hard to prove, some scholars prefer to call them “female figurines with likely cultic significance”.
sections.arts:
Crafts at Mehrgarh grew steadily more skilled. Period I ornaments were made of sea shell, limestone, turquoise, lapis lazuli and sandstone, and there were simple figurines of women and animals. In Period II glazed faience beads were produced and terracotta figurines became more detailed, the women painted and shown with varied hairstyles and ornaments. The first button seals, made of terracotta and bone with geometric designs, also date from this time.

Pottery begins in Period II. In Period III finds become far more abundant as the potter’s wheel is introduced, with more intricate designs and animal motifs. Togau ware appears at the start of Period III: first defined by Beatrice de Cardi in 1948 and named after a mound near Kalat, it is decorated with geometric designs, was already made on the wheel, and is found widely in Balochistan and eastern Afghanistan, at 84 sites according to Possehl. Pipal-leaf designs are used from Period VI, and sophisticated firing techniques in Periods VI and VII. By Period VIII the quality of the designs seems to have suffered from mass production and a growing interest in bronze and copper vessels.

Metalworking began early. A few copper items date from Period IIB, and the technologies of Periods II and III included stone and copper drills, updraft kilns, large pit kilns and crucibles for melting copper; residents made tools from local copper ore. A wheel-shaped copper amulet about 6,000 years old is the oldest known example of the lost-wax technique. It was made of unalloyed copper, an unusual innovation that was later abandoned.
sections.exchange:
Mehrgarh was not isolated. Sea shells from distant coasts and lapis lazuli from as far away as present-day Badakhshan, found in Period I, show contact with those areas, and more beads of Badakhshan lapis lazuli in Period II point to long-distance trade. The similarities between Neolithic sites of eastern Mesopotamia and the western Indus Valley are evidence, in Jarrige’s words, of a “cultural continuum” between them, though he stresses Mehrgarh’s own local background.

Periods II and III coincide with an expansion of settled peoples along the western edge of South Asia, with settlements such as Rana Ghundai, Sheri Khan Tarakai, Sarai Kala, Jalilpur and Ghaligai. In the second half of the 4th millennium BCE the number of settlements rose sharply in the Quetta Valley, the Surab region and the Kachhi Plain, and Togau pottery is found as far as Mundigak in Afghanistan. Much later, the archaeologist Massimo Vidale considers a series of semi-columns in a structure at Mehrgarh, dated around 2500 BCE, to be very similar to semi-columns of Period IV at Shahr-e Sukhteh in Iran.

Studies of teeth and genes point to movements of people. Lukacs and Hemphill found that the Chalcolithic population of Mehrgarh did not descend from its Neolithic population, which suggests “moderate levels of gene flow”. A study of lactose tolerance in India by Gallego Romero and colleagues (2011) suggests that the west Eurasian genetic contribution in India mainly reflects gene flow from Iran and the Middle East, that the commonest lactose-tolerance mutation was likely carried eastward to India along the coast of the Persian Gulf, and notes that the earliest evidence of cattle herding in South Asia comes from Mehrgarh.
sections.legacy:
Mehrgarh’s long occupation ended in the time of the Indus Valley Civilisation. Sometime between 2600 and 2000 BCE, when that civilisation was in its middle stages, the site seems to have been largely abandoned in favour of the larger fortified town of Nausharo, five miles away; the historian Michael Wood suggests that this took place around 2500 BCE. The last period, Period VIII, is known from the Sibri cemetery, about 8 kilometres from Mehrgarh.

Its place in the story of South Asia is discussed. According to Asko Parpola, the culture migrated into the Indus Valley and became the Indus Valley Civilisation of the Bronze Age. Lukacs and Hemphill, from dental evidence, place the direct descendants of its Neolithic people to the south and east, in north-western India and on the western edge of the Deccan Plateau: Neolithic Mehrgarh shows a greater affinity with Chalcolithic Inamgaon than with Chalcolithic Mehrgarh itself.

The site holds several firsts for South Asia: probably the earliest known centre of agriculture, the earliest evidence of cattle herding, the earliest ground stone axes from a stratified context, the oldest ceramic figurines and the oldest evidence of teeth drilled in a living person. Among the works on its finds are the Mehrgarh Field Reports 1974–85, edited by C. and J.-F. Jarrige, R. H. Meadow and G. Quivron, which trace the site from Neolithic times to the Indus Civilisation.

summary: Mehrgarh, on the Kacchi Plain of Balochistan in Pakistan, is one of the earliest farming sites in South Asia, lived in over eight periods from a Neolithic village (dated c. 7000 or c. 5250 BCE) until it was largely abandoned between 2600 and 2000 BCE. Its people grew barley and wheat, herded sheep, goats and cattle, and lived in mud-brick houses. In time they made wheel-thrown decorated pottery, faience beads, seals and copper objects.

notes: Dating conflict kept open in the text: the article gives the first village as 7000 BCE (Jarrige, Period I pre-7000–5500 BCE) or 5250 BCE (Mutin and Zazzo’s radiocarbon dating on teeth, Period I 5250–4650 BCE). Start kept at -7000 as assigned; the editor may prefer -5250 with circa. The 2006 Nature authors date the graveyard to 7,500–9,000 years ago, which fits the older dating.
End kept at -2500: abandonment is given as sometime 2600–2000 BCE (Michael Wood: c. 2500 BCE); Period VIII (Sibri cemetery) is undated in the article.
The article also says the residents of “the later period (5500 BCE to 2600 BCE)”, a range that follows the older chronology; repeated as given.
The article’s external links include “Archaeological Site of Mehrgarh, UNESCO” but the text names no UNESCO listing (it is presumably the Tentative List); no listing claimed.

“Mehrgarh culture” is not a term the article uses; the text explains it as a name taken from the site. Possehl, Wood, Parpola, Lukacs and Hemphill are named as the article names them (no first names for Mutin, Zazzo, Lukacs, Hemphill).
